extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, media scholars, and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating whether journalistic practice is fair — covering ethical behavior, transparency, objectivity, commercial pressures, and institutional reforms to promote trust. Intended as guidance for practitioners, educators, and media institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confessional transparency / visible confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a critical mass of confessional material and publicly acknowledge personal errors or biases (the book's opening section is devoted to confession; "swears to his own hurt").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal tales of misdeeds and angst when teaching or explaining ethics to demonstrate authenticity; make admissions of mistakes visible so the public can see reporters and editors 'swear to our own hurt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting personal admiration or bias cloud news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reporters must prevent personal feelings about subjects from influencing coverage (example: Tom Winship's admiration of John F. Kennedy led to a premature 'Kennedy Wins' headline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to how admiration, affinity, or other emotions can produce erroneous editorial decisions; institutional safeguards or self-scrutiny can mitigate these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and scrutinize use of unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about overreliance on unnamed sources (David Shaw discovered he had used more unnamed sources than he wanted to remember).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate necessity, corroboration, and transparency for anonymous sourcing; excessive use can undermine accountability and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harming innocent sources; minimize unintentional damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should take care not to cause unintended hurt to sources (Walter Anderson agonized over unintentionally hurting an innocent source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh potential harm in reporting decisions, issue corrections/apologies when harm occurs, and adopt policies to protect vulnerable sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand historical and business origins of professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that modern journalistic professionalism grew from a business model aimed at mass audiences and that different systems (e.g., narrower party-oriented European journalism) yield different outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical perspective to evaluate how institutional incentives shaped norms and consider whether those incentives still apply under new technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend commitment to objective truth against social constructivism
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist intellectual currents that negate objectivity — social constructivist views that 'reality is socially constructed' can moot the issue of fairness because 'If truth is whatever works for you, there is no need for journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirm the role of truth-seeking in journalism; scrutinize theoretical approaches that could justify partisan spin or relativism in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject training journalists as 'spin doctors'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid educating journalists to create spin rather than report facts (the author warns that teaching young to be spin doctors has become an accepted goal in some programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and newsroom practices should emphasize verification, context, and fair presentation rather than manipulation and advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for commercial pressures that undermine fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that profit motives and short-term accounting (e.g., saving newsprint) can corrupt fairness; market pressures may either harm or incentivize improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how economic incentives shape editorial choices; look for business models or management practices that can align profitability with fairness and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat trust as predictable behavior with economic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust derives from predictable behavior and has long-term economic value; information providers that reliably satisfy audiences can capture a durable market advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in consistent, trustworthy practices even if payoff is slow; consider trust-building as a strategic asset rather than a cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek business-model innovations that reward fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Find or design media products and business models that capture the economic value of fairness so owners can 'do well and do good at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with products/services that monetize trust (e.g., subscriptions, branded verification) and measure whether fair practices can be financially sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt formal professionalism and peer review to identify unfair practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement systems of peer review designed to publicly identify specific unfair practices as part of a more formal professionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create transparent, public mechanisms (peer review panels, ombudsmen, ethics audits) that document and call out unfair behavior in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain separation between journalism and corrupting influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep traditional journalism distinct in the public mind from corrupting influences of both postmodernist relativism and financial 'money-changers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate clearly about journalistic standards and institutional safeguards so audiences can distinguish trustworthy news from spin or commercial manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accountability through visible admission and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Make accountability visible (e.g., public confessions, corrections) so the profession demonstrates willingness to 'swear to our own hurt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize public corrections, editor's notes, and ethics reporting to show transparency and commitment to fairness.
